column11: measured on the same beneficiaries the price is quoted on. CMS Part B 2024 (drug_demand): 59,614,546 dosage units over 52,146 beneficiaries = 1,143.2 mg each, and J3111 is 'injection, romosozumab-aqqg, 1 mg'. The label caps treatment at 12 monthly 210 mg doses, so a full labelled course and a full labelled year are both 2,520 mg; a beneficiary averages 0.4537 of it and 1 - 0.4537 = 0.5463. The ratio is stable across 2020 to 2024 (0.463, 0.437, 0.447, 0.454, 0.454). Internal check: 59,614,546 mg at 210 mg a dose is 283,879 doses against 285,908 claims in the same file, within 0.7%, so a claim is a dose and a beneficiary averages 5.48 of the 12. Published cross-check: Soen S, Wang A, Hamaya E, Chien HC, Lin TC, J Bone Miner Metab 2024;42(6):653-667, doi 10.1007/s00774-024-01530-6, PMID 38987505 (Japanese claims, 13,694 romosozumab initiators across the Medical Data Vision and Japan Medical Data Center databases) reports 12-month romosozumab discontinuation of 62.4% and 58.8% in MDV and 57.1% and 52.7% in JMDC across the launch-year and second-year cohorts, which brackets the 54.6% measured here, and a mean of 9.7, 9.8, 7.3 and 7.8 injections over 12 months against the 9.96 this rate implies (1/0.5463 = 1.83 beneficiary-years at 5.44 doses each)
column12: Judgement on method, stated: romosozumab is a capped 12-month course, so a patient who completes it stops because the label says to, not because the disease resolved. The measured rate is not 1.0 because the course is monthly and straddles a calendar year end: a patient starting in July bills six doses in each of two years. That is why this is read off dosage units rather than set to 1.0, which is what the book does for a 51-week course that cannot straddle a year end. The case against: a sequential-therapy patient who moves to denosumab or a bisphosphonate after 12 doses is counted here as a stop, which is correct for this product and understates the franchise

column11: no US population-based prevalence of osteogenesis imperfecta is published, so a national registry rate from elsewhere is applied to the US population and labelled as such. Storoni S, Treurniet S, Maugeri A et al., 'Prevalence and Hospital Admissions in Patients With Osteogenesis Imperfecta in The Netherlands: A Nationwide Registry Study', Front Endocrinol 2022;13:869604, doi 10.3389/fendo.2022.869604, PMID 35546999, give a point prevalence of 0.005%, 5.0 per 100,000, in the general Dutch population at April 2021. Applied to the 341,784,857 US residents at 2025-07-01 (Census Vintage 2025, NC-EST2025-AGESEX-RES, both sexes, POPESTIMATE2025, www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/national/asrh/nc-est2025-agesex-res.csv, downloaded and summed 2026-10-27): 3,417.84857 x 5.0 = 17,089
column12: the book held no pool for this disease, and this is the weakest pool in the file. The published band is wide: a Turkish national e-health registry brackets the literature at 4 to 20 per 100,000 (Gorgun B et al., J Pediatr Orthop B 2025;34, doi 10.1097/bpb.0000000000001192, PMID 38900105), which on the same denominator is 13,671 to 68,357. MedlinePlus Genetics asserts 25,000 to 50,000 US patients but cites nothing for it and contradicts its own 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 20,000 rate, which gives 17,089 to 34,178; the Dutch registry figure sits at the bottom of that, so this row leans LOW. column11: two shares multiplied against the enrolment criteria of NCT05972551, which takes ambulatory children and adolescents aged 5 to under 18 with clinical type I, III or IV osteogenesis imperfecta who meet at least one of three fracture criteria: 3 or more fractures in the previous 2 years, 1 or more nonvertebral fracture plus at least 1 prevalent vertebral fracture, or 2 or more prevalent vertebral fractures. (1) Children aged 5 to 17 are 23.18% of the prevalent pool. Lindahl K, Astrom E, Rubin CJ, Grigelioniene G, Malmgren B, Ljunggren O, Kindmark A, 'Genetic epidemiology, prevalence, and genotype-phenotype correlations in the Swedish population with osteogenesis imperfecta', Eur J Hum Genet 2015;23(8):1042-1050, doi 10.1038/ejhg.2015.81, PMID 25944380, give a point prevalence of 7.40 per 100,000 among Swedish children under 18 (142 children in a denominator of 1,919,094 at 2010-12-31). Applied to the 53,529,481 US residents aged 5 to 17 (same Census file as the pool row): 535.29481 x 7.40 = 3,961 children, which is 3,961 / 17,089 = 0.2318. (2) The severity gate is taken at 32%, the share of US paediatric osteogenesis imperfecta patients who actually receive a bone treatment: Yang EC, Cigeroglu O, Gupta RN et al., JBMR Plus 2025;9(10):ziaf124, doi 10.1093/jbmrpl/ziaf124, PMID 40978118 (IQVIA PharMetrics Plus, January 2016 to February 2020, 2,095 US osteogenesis imperfecta patients) report that patients under 18 were the most likely to receive a treatment of interest, at 32%, against 24.3% across all ages, with bisphosphonates 21.1% and romosozumab 0%. 0.2318 x 0.32 = 0.074174, about 1,268 US children
column12: Judgement on the second share, and it is the row to argue with. The protocol screens on fracture burden, not on Sillence type, and no published distribution of the fracture criterion exists; the measured share of paediatric patients a US physician already treats with an off-label bone agent is the closest observable thing to the same triage, and it is what the bisphosphonate control arm is drawn from. A strict reading of the fracture criterion alone would give less: Yang reports about 40% of patients had a fracture within one year of diagnosis and 33% of paediatric patients with fractures had more than three fractures within a year, and more than three in one year must satisfy three in two years, so 0.40 x 0.33 = 0.132 is a lower bound by construction. The pool is also not cut for ambulatory status or for the COL1A1 or COL1A2 requirement that excludes types V and above, both of which would reduce it. Mixing a Dutch all-age rate with a Swedish paediatric rate is itself a weakness: it implies 23.2% of patients are aged 5 to 17 where the two US claims cohorts read 35.1% and 47.1% under 18, so the age share may be low

column11: a judgement. No drug is approved for osteogenesis imperfecta in the US: bisphosphonates, the comparator arm of NCT05972551, are used off label, which is why the trial can randomise against them, and Yang EC et al. (JBMR Plus 2025;9(10):ziaf124) measure romosozumab use in US osteogenesis imperfecta at 0%. A first approved therapy in a disease with none, in a severity-selected paediatric pool managed at a small number of specialist centres, takes a high share of the patients who qualify
column12: a judgement that nothing resolves except years of sales, so no replacement clause is offered. The case for lower: romosozumab carries a boxed warning for myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death, and the label caps use at 12 monthly doses, so a prescriber is choosing one year of treatment and then something else, against generic bisphosphonates at a fraction of $12,261. The case for higher: 0.3 of the eligible pool is about 380 US children, which a single-digit number of specialist centres could reach. Note the eligible pool is already defined as the children a physician treats, so this is a share of a treated population rather than of everyone with the disease

column11: a different disease and a different age. EVENITY is indicated for the treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk for fracture, and the label states that safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients (openFDA drug/label). NCT05972551 enrols children and adolescents 5 to under 18 with osteogenesis imperfecta, a heritable collagen disorder rather than postmenopausal bone loss. a judgement, set well below the published chain on purpose. The published figure, for reference, is the rare-disease cut of the BIO / Informa Pharma Intelligence / QLS Advisors 'Clinical Development Success Rates and Contributing Factors 2011-2020' report, Figure 8b page 14, ahead of a Phase 3 readout: 0.604 Phase 3 to NDA/BLA on 240 transitions and 0.936 NDA/BLA to approval on 172, which is 0.5653. What takes it down is a stated result on the same mechanism in the same disease. Ultragenyx 8-K of 2025-12-29 (0001193125-25-332422, Item 8.01) on setrusumab, the other anti-sclerostin antibody in osteogenesis imperfecta: 'Neither study achieved statistical significance against the primary endpoints of reduction in annualized clinical fracture rate compared to placebo or bisphosphonates, respectively. Both studies achieved the secondary endpoints of improvements in bone mineral density ('BMD') against comparators.' Earlier, in adults, setrusumab also missed: Glorieux FH et al., 'Setrusumab for the treatment of osteogenesis imperfecta: 12-month results from the phase 2b ASTEROID study', J Bone Miner Res 2024;39(9):1215-1228, doi 10.1093/jbmr/zjae112, PMID 39012717, report that the primary endpoint of change in radial trabecular volumetric BMD at month 12 did not reach statistical significance, while several secondary bone measures did. NCT05972551 has three co-primary endpoints, number of clinical fractures at 12 months, number of any fractures at 12 months and change in lumbar spine BMD Z-score; two of the three are the endpoint that has just failed on this mechanism and one is the kind it passed, and 111 participants over 12 months is a small fracture-count trial
column12: Replace this with 0.936, the NDA to approval rate above, if Amgen reports a positive readout at the 2027-05-04 primary completion, or with 0 if it reports a miss. The case for higher than 0.25: Cosmic, the paediatric setrusumab study against bisphosphonates, showed a numerical fracture reduction and failed only on significance in patients with a higher baseline fracture rate than Orbit's, and NCT05972551 screens on fracture history the same way; Amgen's own Phase 1 in 25 children (NCT04545554, results posted 2023-10-18) raised lumbar spine areal BMD 7.1% to 15.0% over 169 days; and the BMD co-primary is a route to approval that does not need the fracture endpoint. The case for lower: an open-label trial against an active comparator in 111 children is not a design that rescues a fracture endpoint
